theory.overview: Quantum computers threaten current cryptography. Shor's algorithm breaks RSA, DSA, and ECDSA in polynomial time on quantum computers. Grover's algorithm halves symmetric key security but is manageable with larger keys. Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) develops algorithms secure against both classical and quantum attacks. NIST's 2024 PQC standards—CRYSTALS-Kyber for key encapsulation and CRYSTALS-Dilithium for signatures—mark the beginning of the quantum-resistant era. Understanding PQC is essential for long-term security planning.

sections.title: The Quantum Threat
sections.content: Quantum computers use qubits and quantum algorithms to solve certain problems exponentially faster. Shor's algorithm factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time, completely breaking RSA and ECC. A few thousand logical qubits could break 2048-bit RSA. Current quantum computers have hundreds of noisy qubits—not yet capable, but advancing rapidly. Harvest now, decrypt later: attackers may record encrypted traffic today to decrypt when quantum computers mature. This creates urgency for PQC adoption even before quantum computers exist.

sections.title: Lattice-Based Cryptography
sections.content: Lattice-based cryptography is the leading PQC approach. Built on hard lattice problems like Learning With Errors (LWE) and Ring-LWE. These problems resist quantum attacks because they're based on high-dimensional geometry rather than number theory. CRYSTALS-Kyber (now ML-KEM) provides IND-CCA2 secure key encapsulation with reasonable key sizes (~1KB) and performance comparable to ECDH. CRYSTALS-Dilithium (now ML-DSA) provides signatures. Lattice problems have security proofs reducing to worst-case hard problems, providing confidence in their security.

sections.title: Other PQC Approaches
sections.content: Beyond lattices, multiple approaches exist. Hash-based signatures (SPHINCS+) are conservative, based only on hash function security with no number-theoretic assumptions—slow but trusted. Code-based cryptography (Classic McEliece) uses error-correcting codes, large keys but well-studied. Multivariate cryptography uses systems of quadratic equations. Isogeny-based cryptography (SIKE) was broken in 2022, demonstrating PQC risks. NIST continues evaluating additional candidates for future standards.

sections.title: Migration Strategies
sections.content: Transitioning to PQC requires planning. Hybrid approaches combine classical and post-quantum algorithms during transition—if PQC fails, classical still protects. Google's 2016 experiment combined ECDH with NewHope. Key size increases: Kyber public keys are ~1KB vs 32 bytes for X25519, impacting bandwidth. Performance: Kyber is fast but signatures (Dilithium) add overhead. Algorithm agility: design systems to swap algorithms. Crypto inventory: identify all uses of vulnerable algorithms. NIST recommends starting migration now, with full transition by 2035.

steps.title: Assess Current Cryptography
steps.description: Inventory all uses of RSA, DSA, ECDSA, and DH.

steps.title: Select PQC Algorithms
steps.description: Choose NIST-approved algorithms: ML-KEM for KEM, ML-DSA for signatures.

steps.title: Hybrid Deployment
steps.description: Deploy hybrid classical + PQC during transition period.

steps.title: Update Infrastructure
steps.description: Update TLS libraries, certificates, and key management.

steps.title: Monitor Standards
steps.description: Follow NIST updates and cryptoanalytic developments.

practiceProblems.title: Shor's Algorithm Target
practiceProblems.description: Which algorithms does Shor's algorithm break?

solution.explanation: Shor's algorithm efficiently factors integers and solves discrete logarithms, breaking all algorithms based on these problems.

practiceProblems.title: Grover's Impact
practiceProblems.description: What is the impact of Grover's algorithm on symmetric cryptography?

solution.explanation: Grover's algorithm searches unsorted databases in O(sqrt(N)), effectively halving key security. AES-256 becomes ~128-bit secure—still secure, but AES-128 becomes ~64-bit—unsafe.

practiceProblems.title: Hybrid Approach
practiceProblems.description: Why use hybrid classical + post-quantum during transition?

solution.answer: Protects against both classical and quantum attacks; fallback if PQC breaks
solution.explanation: Hybrids ensure that if the PQC algorithm has an undiscovered weakness, the classical component still provides security. This is conservative during the transition period.

snippets.title: Kyber KEM (Conceptual)
snippets.code:
# Using liboqs or similar PQC library
from oqs import KeyEncapsulation

kem = KeyEncapsulation('Kyber512')
public_key = kem.generate_keypair()

# Encapsulate: creates ciphertext and shared secret
ciphertext, shared_secret = kem.encap_secret(public_key)

# Decapsulate: recovers shared secret
recovered = kem.decap_secret(ciphertext)
